newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury mart looks at fundamentals, turns blue.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury mart looks at fundamentals, turns blue.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market is turning its eyes back to economic fundamentals after spending several weeks trading mostly on technical factors and foreign capital inflows, Wall Street pundits said.
But market participants do not appear to be pleased with what they see.
The latest batch of economic indicators suggested the U.S. economy might be growing at a somewhat stronger pace than previously thought, trigerring a major selloff across the Treasury yield curve.
"There is a shift in sentiment in the market," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
The change in the market's mood began when Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan said in a speech early in December that the Fed must be wary when "irrational exuberance" affects stocks and assets.
At the time, Greenspan also said U.S. inflation has been low recently, but the future course was uncertain.
Analysts said the Fed chief's remarks cast a shadow on the market's belief that interest rates were to remain mostly unchanged with no inflationary pressures in 1997.
Some of the economic data that followed Greenspan's comments were not market-friendly, analysts noted.

October business inventories rose 0.5 percent after a 0.1 percent increase in September. November industrial production jumped a surprising 0.9 percent against a 0.2 percent drop in the previous month.
U.S. housing starts surged a strong 9.2 percent in November to a 1.514 million unit annual rate after a 5.1 percent drop in October.
On top of that, anecdotal retail sales data as measured by weekly chain store indices hinted that the holiday shopping season might be fairly strong.

The combination of Greenspan's remarks and data boosted the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond to the current 6.65 percent against the 6.36 percent registered at the close of business on December 2.
"This is indicative of a change in psychology in the last several weeks ... People are now much more cautious," said Lee Youngdahl, vice-president and an economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc.

"The preponderence of opinions now is that things are starting to firm up somewhat. The statistics show that ... the (economic) outlook for the first part of next year has improved somewhat," Youngdahl said.
But does this shift in sentiment mean the market now expects the Fed to tighten monetary policy soon?

"I wouldn't say that we've come to the point now that people are looking for a tightening. But we have come to the point where people are beginning to contemplate the possibility of a tightening," HSBC's Low said.

The Fed's policy-setting arm, the Federal Open Market Committee, decided to leave interest rates unchanged at its meeting on December 17. The central bank's decision was in line with market expectations.
The Fed last changed interest rates in February, when it trimmed its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5.25 percent.
Some analysts, however, attributed the market's current pessimism to more technical factors.

"You have a situation where you have impending supply and an end-of-year temptation to take profits, so any piece of strong (economic) news will be used to sell the market," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities.
The Treasury will offer the market $18.25 billion of two-year notes in a formal auction on Wednesday and $12.5 billion of five-year notes during a sale on Thursday.
